newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief laments shrinking interest in world news.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief laments shrinking interest in world news.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali lamented on Tuesday what he said was a shrinking interest in international news, saying the average citizen's knowledge of serious world affairs had diminished.

"There are far fewer 'foreign correspondents' or overseas news bureaux. Editors and publishers say they cannot afford them. They say the public just isn't very interested in what's happening elsewhere in the world."

Addressing a lunch given by U.N. correspondents, he said that, while there was still a lot of international news, all too often it featured "only the most dramatic -- or the most horrible -- events," which could still arouse great interest and inflame emotions.

"But with the decline in sustained interest in international news, these big events lack context. Without continuous coverage of an issue or a geographic area, big news that suddenly bursts into the media is extremely hard to judge or to comprehend.
"As a result, public opinion can become public pressure for action that is not well founded," he said, without citing specific examples.
"And then, just as suddenly as it came, the story is gone," said Boutros-Ghali, whose re-election for a second five-year term is opposed by the United States.
The "marvellous global television networks" could serve to counteract this trend, he said.

"But often they are the means not of carrying solid news of international affairs in a comprehensive way, but of transmitting material about the developed world to the developing world rather than the other way around."

The United Nations was affected since, although located in what was perhaps the media capital of the world, "we face a daily struggle to ensure that our message is heard and reported fairly and accurately," Boutros-Ghali said.
"As journalists, you face a daily struggle to ensure that serious copy is used and that coverage is not dominated by trivia and merely entertaining material," he told his audience.
"Unfortunately, this is a struggle we both appear to be losing," he said, and it could only have a negative impact on diplomacy and international relations."
